paragraphs.heading: What the trade was
paragraphs.text: The Atlantic slave trade was the business of shipping enslaved African people across the ocean to the Americas. Slave ships based both in Europe and in the New World carried it out. Europeans set up a slave trade along the African coast in the 1400s, and shipments to the Americas started in the 1500s and went on well into the 1800s. Most of the people taken came from Central and West Africa.

paragraphs.heading: The scale of it
paragraphs.text: By current estimates, slave ships took on about 12.75 million Africans for the crossing to the Americas, and as many as 2 million of them died on the way. Ranked by how much they traded, Portugal came first, then Britain and Spain, with France, the Netherlands, the United States and Denmark behind them. The biggest slave ports were in South America, and ships based in the New World probably carried more captives than ships from European home ports. Early in the 1800s several governments moved to ban the trade, though smuggling carried on.

paragraphs.heading: How captives were bought
paragraphs.text: In contrast to other slave trades, the people taking captives out of Africa usually bought them from West and Central African slave merchants. Europeans did take part in some raids, but this was rare and discouraged. At their African slaving bases the Portuguese built barracoons, where newly bought captives were gathered to wait for the next ship. Northern European traders more often used the ship itself as the base, so their ships stayed far longer on the coast and the first people bought were held on board longer.

paragraphs.heading: Why the Americas wanted labour
paragraphs.text: After Australia, the Americas were far more thinly populated than the other inhabited continents. The European conquerors needed workers, but the small native population was shrinking from European diseases, and Europeans themselves were reluctant to emigrate at that early stage. They turned to the answer already used on the sugar plantations of Madeira and the Canary Islands around 1450: slaves brought from Africa south of the Sahara. Enslaved Africans were put to work on plantations of sugar, cotton, tobacco, coffee and cocoa, in rice fields and mines, in building and timber cutting, and as skilled workers or house servants.

paragraphs.heading: From servant to property
paragraphs.text: In the English colonies, the earliest enslaved Africans to arrive were classed as indentured servants, with a legal standing like that of contract workers from Britain and Ireland. By the mid-1600s this had hardened into a racial caste system of chattel slavery. Under it, enslaved Africans and their future children were legally their owners' property, and a child born to an enslaved mother was also counted as enslaved. As property, people were sold at market like other goods, with prices set by their health and how much work buyers expected from them.

paragraphs.heading: Older trades and a new market
paragraphs.text: Slavery had been common in many parts of Africa for centuries before the Atlantic trade, and a trade across the Sahara had run since ancient times. Europeans usually bought people who had been captured in the constant wars between African states, trading muskets, cloth or alcohol for them. European demand made this existing trade bigger. Someone enslaved within their own region might hope to escape, but those shipped across the ocean had little chance of ever going home.
